item.title: Lab 1: MNIST From Pixels to a Neural Network — What Do the Weights Actually Represent?
item.description:
Lab 1: What Do the Weights of a Neural Network Actually Represent?

MNIST internals series — the practical companion to the ML notes (softmax & cross-entropy, backprop, training a 2-layer network). This time we stop deriving and start looking.

Anyone who has trained a model eventually asks:

The model is just a pile of numbers. In this lab’s case, exactly 7,860 of them (7,850 weights + 10 biases). What do those numbers actually mean?

item.title: Lab 2: Teach It 1s and 2s First, Then Introduce 3 — Watching Weights Reorganize
item.description:
Lab 2: Teach It 1s and 2s First, Then Introduce 3 — Watching Weights Reorganize

MNIST internals series. In Lab 1 we established what a weight row is: a learned photograph of a class, contrast-carved against its rivals, painted by the update rule $W_c \leftarrow W_c - \eta\,\tfrac1N\sum (\hat p_c - y_c)\,x^\top$ .

Now the experiment that motivated the series: start the model in an impoverished world — only 1s and 2s exist — then let it discover 3. This is continual learning in miniature, and it lets us watch, directly and quantitatively:
